# Esther 7: research notes, verse by verse

**Before you use these notes:** I ran out of search and page-read allowance partway through, so some areas are thin. Most material comes from older commentaries on biblehub.com and studylight.org, plus Guzik's commentary on enduringword.com. Things I could not find are listed at the end.

---

**v. 1–2 (the second banquet; "up to half the kingdom")**
- Matthew Henry describes ch. 7 simply as the second banquet, where Esther asks for her life and her people's. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Est/Est_007.cfm We are now to attend the second banquet to which the king and Haman were invited: and there,. I. Esther presents her petition to the king for her life and the life of her people (v. 1-4).
- Adam Clarke reads vv. 1–2 as the king urging her to make her request with the positive assurance that it shall be granted. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/esther-7.html

**v. 3 (Esther's petition)**
- Guzik says she was tactful. At first she did not say she was a Jew, just as Haman had hidden which people he meant to destroy (3:8). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/esther-7/
- He also says she was wise to make it personal. Her appeal rests on her own standing, since she had only ever pleased the king. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/esther-7/
- One writer on Bible Hub sees God's providence at work. He says the king's heart was in God's hand and was being "turned" as God saw best. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/esther/7-4.htm

**v. 4 ("sold… destroyed, killed, annihilated"; the hard final clause)**
- **"Sold":** Several commentators say this points to Haman's bribe of 10,000 talents (3:9; 4:7). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/esther/7-4.htm. The Preacher's Homiletical Commentary agrees. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/esther-7.html
- **The three verbs:** Clarke says Esther repeats the exact words of Haman's decree (3:13). https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/esther-7.html. The Pulpit Commentary says the three near-synonyms are not wordiness but stress how complete the destruction would be. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/esther-7.html
- **The last clause is genuinely unclear, and commentators split:**
  - *Reading A (the KJV sense): Haman's money could never make up for the king's loss.* The Geneva notes say Haman's malice could not benefit the king as much as losing the Jews and their tribute would harm him. https://www.ccel.org/g/geneva/notes/Esther/7.html. Barnes takes the same view. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/esther/7-4.html. So does Clarke: even 10,000 talents could not replace a whole nation for all its generations. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/esther/7-4.html
  - *Reading B (the BSB/NET sense): the matter would not have been worth troubling the king about.* Keil and Delitzsch say Esther would have kept quiet about mere slavery, because the enemy was not worth bothering the king over. The Pulpit Commentary calls Bertheau's similar reading "simpler, and perhaps better." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/esther/7-4.htm
  - The Preacher's Homiletical Commentary suggests Esther may have *meant* the sentence to be ambiguous. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/esther-7.html
  - Gill notes that the Jewish commentator Aben Ezra and some others take the word usually read "enemy" to mean "distress." https://www.studylight.org/commentary/esther/7-4.html
- **Application:** Coffman says Esther put all the blame on Haman and left out the king's own part in the decree. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/esther/7-4.html

**v. 5 ("Who is he?")**
- Guzik points out the irony: the king himself had approved the plot (3:10–11), though he did not understand it. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/esther-7/
- John Brown asks whether Xerxes had so quickly forgotten his own part, and notes that we see others' sins more easily than our own. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/brown_john/Est/Esther_07.cfm
- Barnes says the king perhaps learned only now that his queen was Jewish. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/esther/7-4.html

**v. 6 ("this wicked man — Haman!")**
- Guzik says Haman is exposed as no faithful servant but an enemy chasing his own fame. He adds that the purpose of Esther's two banquets now becomes clear: they made the blow land hardest. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/esther-7/
- Matthew Henry pictures the scene as a court: the queen accuses, the king judges, and Haman's own conscience testifies against him. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Est/Est_007.cfm

**v. 7 (the king goes to the garden; Haman pleads)**
- Guzik thinks the king's anger came partly from realising Haman had made a fool of him. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/esther-7/
- The Geneva notes say Haman's conscience told him God's vengeance would fall on him for plotting the death of innocent people. https://www.ccel.org/g/geneva/notes/Esther/7.html
- Matthew Henry draws a lesson: when angry, we should pause before deciding anything. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Est/Est_007.cfm

**v. 8 (Haman falls on the couch; his face is covered)**
- **The posture:** Barnes explains that Persians, like Greeks and Romans, ate lying on couches, and Haman had thrown himself at Esther's feet. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/esther/7-9.htm. Poole thinks Haman was on his knees beside the couch, as a suppliant. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/esther/7-8.htm
- **Did the king really think it was an assault?** Most say no. Gill, Henry, Clarke and Coffman all say the king put the worst possible meaning on what he saw in order to vent his anger. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/esther/7-8.html and https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/esther-7.html. Another writer on Bible Hub says the king must have known Haman was simply begging. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/esther/7-8.htm
- A different emphasis: Constable says strict rules surrounded the royal harem, so the king's reaction could be justified even if Haman knelt a foot away. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/esther/7-8.html. The Light of Israel commentary (quoting Utley) says any approach to the king's wife was taboo in Persia. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/esther/7-7.html
- **Covering the face:** Guzik reads this as preparation for execution. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/esther-7/. The Geneva notes call it the Persian custom when someone lost the king's favour. https://www.ccel.org/g/geneva/notes/Esther/7.html. Barnes compares Macedonian and Roman practice. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/esther/7-9.htm
- **Jewish tradition:** Guzik mentions a Jewish writing in which the angel Gabriel pushed Haman onto the couch. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/esther-7/

**v. 9 (Harbonah and the gallows)**
- **Who Harbonah was:** Gill says he was one of the seven chamberlains of 1:10. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/esther/7-9.htm. Jamieson-Fausset-Brown suggest he had been sent to fetch Haman and had seen the gallows then. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/esther/7-9.htm
- **His motive:** Henry says the courtiers who flattered Haman now turned on him as a "falling star." https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Est/Est_007.cfm
- **Haman's added guilt:** Gill says Haman built a gallows for a man who had not been accused or condemned, and who had saved the king's life. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/esther/7-9.htm
- **The height:** Coffman thinks a 50-cubit (about 75 ft) structure at a house is unlikely. He suggests the gallows stood on the city wall and was 50 cubits "high" in the sense of its elevation. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/esther/7-8.html
- **Hanging or impaling?** Guzik says Haman was probably impaled on a stake, an early form of crucifixion, rather than hanged with a rope. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/esther-7/. Ellicott notes that the Greek Septuagint says "let him be crucified." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/esther/7-9.htm

**v. 10 (Haman hanged; the king's wrath subsides)**
- **Getting what he planned for others:** Commentators widely cite Psalm 7:15–16 and 9:15. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/esther-7/ and https://www.studylight.org/commentary/esther/7-8.html. Henry says Haman was justly hanged on the very gallows he had unjustly prepared for Mordecai. He adds that in the morning Mordecai faced the gallows, but now Mordecai has the crown, Haman the cross. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Est/Est_007.cfm
- **Pointing to Christ:** Guzik says Satan thought the cross was his victory, but it became his defeat. He also contrasts the two deaths: here the guilty dies instead of the innocent, while at the cross the innocent dies for the guilty. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/esther-7/
- **Where it happened:** Gill thinks it was probably in Haman's courtyard. He also cites the Greek additions, which say Haman was hanged at the gates of Susa. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/esther/7-10.htm
- **A critical view of the king:** A sermon on Bible Hub says the episode shows a fickle tyrant sending Haman to death without any trial. https://biblehub.com/sermons/esther/7-10.htm. Henry likewise notes Haman was not even asked to speak in his defence. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Est/Est_007.cfm
- **Not chance:** The same sermon says putting this reversal down to mere chance "would be the height of folly." https://biblehub.com/sermons/esther/7-10.htm

---

## Where Protestant traditions differ
I found no real disagreement between denominations on this chapter. Teachers from different traditions agree on God's providence, the theme of reversal, and Haman being caught in his own trap. Examples: the Geneva notes (Reformed), https://www.ccel.org/g/geneva/notes/Esther/7.html; Gill (Baptist), https://biblehub.com/commentaries/esther/7-10.htm; Guzik (Calvary Chapel-style), https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/esther-7/. MacArthur says Esther is the classic picture of God's providence, even though God is never named. https://www.gty.org/library/Bible-Introductions/MSB17/Esther. The disagreements I did find are about how to translate v. 4 and how to read the king's outburst in v. 8, not about doctrine.

## Other views
- **The Greek additions (Catholic and Orthodox):** The Wesley Center explains that the Greek text adds 107 verses that mention God about 50 times. Catholic and Orthodox Bibles include them in Esther; Protestants place them in the Apocrypha. https://wesley.nnu.edu/sermons-essays-books/noncanonical-literature/noncanonical-literature-ot-apocrypha/additions-to-esther/
- **Catholic reading of this scene:** Catholic.com reads the Greek text as saying God moved the king to change his mind, so Haman's scaffold was used on Haman. It says the Hebrew book is still filled with a sense of providence. https://www.catholic.com/magazine/print-edition/judith-and-esther. The Douay-Rheims version of v. 4 ends differently, saying the enemy's cruelty "redoundeth upon the king." https://biblehub.com/esther/7-4.htm
- **Modern scholarship:** Bible Odyssey says few scholars think the book is historical; most read it as historical fiction about Jewish life in the Persian diaspora. https://www.bibleodyssey.org/articles/esther/
- **Why God goes unnamed:** The Gospel Coalition commentary argues that leaving God unnamed is deliberate, and that adding him in, as the Greek does, "misses the point." https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/commentary/esther/

## Not found
- NET Bible notes. I only saw the NET's translation of v. 4 ("would not have been sufficient for troubling the king") in a parallel-versions list.
- Any Orthodox (oca.org) material.
- Anything from Lutheran, Methodist or Pentecostal teachers on this chapter specifically.
- Any prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace teaching on Esther 7.

The closest thing to popular teaching was one line in Smith's Bible Commentary on v. 4: God won't allow any weapon formed against you to prosper. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/esther/7-4.html
